doc_summary: Steinhardt argues technically skilled people should build technology (measurement and cost-reduction) that drives AI governance, drawing analogies from climate, food safety, and COVID. He highlights behavioral benchmarks, cheap agent evaluation, and privacy-preserving audit tools as key needs.

items.claim: prefers standardized, reproducible evaluation suites over developer-defined self-measurement because results otherwise cannot be compared or enforced.
items.quote: without reproducible evaluation suites, such requirements are difficult to enforce: developers largely define how their own systems are measured, making results hard to compare.

items.claim: Believes the most valuable evaluations to build target complex agentic behaviors, subtle failures of judgment, and long-horizon deception rather than the toxicity/hallucination issues the mass market focuses on.
items.quote: demand for these harder evaluation tasks (complex agentic behaviors, subtle failures of judgment, deceptive patterns over long horizons) is growing but still emerging; the mass market tends to focus on toxicity, hallucinations, or compliance-related issues.

items.claim: Distrusts ad hoc, unsystematic measurement of behavioral issues like sycophancy, deception, and delusion reinforcement, since these lack public, comparable metrics.
items.quote: We lack good public metrics for sycophancy, deception, reinforcement of delusions, and similar behavioral issues, which are currently measured ad hoc, if at all.

items.claim: prefers cheap, scalable analysis of agent runs over person-months of manual evaluation because expensive evaluation cannot become ubiquitous, while quality must be preserved.
items.quote: METR often spends person-months of work on a single evaluation suite, due to the labor involved in human baselining, running many trials, and manually analyzing results to understand why agents succeed or fail.

items.claim: Chooses what to build by asking whether a technology creates visibility, shifts incentives, or lowers costs, targeting areas before the market tips.
items.quote: That's what makes it high-leverage to push on complex oversight tasks now, similarly to early solar investment before the market tipped.

items.claim: Treats public behavioral benchmarks as competitive-pressure mechanisms, so claims about model behavior should be measurable and comparable across labs.
items.quote: High-quality public dashboards for behavioral issues could do the same, just as fuel efficiency became a selling point for automakers once EPA ratings became standardized.

items.claim: Open problem: confidential auditing technologies (enclaves, cryptographic proofs, structured access) to enable deployment audits without exposing IP.
items.quote: Secure enclaves could let auditors run analyses without extracting underlying weights. Cryptographic methods could let companies prove properties about their training process without revealing proprietary details.

items.claim: prefers measurement of real-world deployment behavior (audits of logs and deployment) over developer-reported claims because external verification enables accountability.
items.quote: we'd like to be able to audit whether AI systems behave badly in deployment, verify claims about training practices, and conduct white-box safety analyses.
